Formalization of the algebraic theory of finite semigroups

Throughout the academic year now ending, I have been working with a team of Boston College students (Nathan Hart-Hodgson, Soleil Repple and Ayden Lamparski) on formalizing a significant portion of the algebraic structure theory of (mostly) finite semigroups.  The principal application of this theory is in the study of finite automata and formal languages, where it is an important tool in classifying regular languages and in determining the expressive power of various restrictions and extensions of first-order logic on words. 

We have completed the formalization of all of the so-called ‘local’ theory that we set out to cover: this includes idempotents, ideals, Green’s relations, groups in semigroups, and the Rees-Suschkewitch theorem, which proves a matrix-like representation of the semigroup’s structure. We mostly worked from two books by Jean-Eric Pin (‘Varieties of Formal Languages’, and ‘Mathematical Foundations of Automata Theory’) that present this material.  Most of the remaining work is cleaning up some of the messier parts of the proofs and improving the documentation.

In a separate project, Ayden Lamparski has formalized the algebra of deterministic finite automata and algorithm for minimizing such automata, which is used to associate a finite semigroup to an automaton.  It is hoped that these projects wo;; provide the basis for further work that will cover the ‘global’ theory (in particular, the wreath product and the Krohn-Rhodes theorem, and the Factorization Forest Theorem) and formalize some of the key results on formal languages.  Ayden has communicated over Zulip about the possible inclusion of this work in CSLib.

We are looking for an appropriate place to contribute this work, whether it be in Mathlib, CSLib, or elsewhere. While the main application is in theoretical computer science, the mathematical content is entirely independent of this, and, in fact, the portion of theory that we have formalized dates back to the 1940’s and 1950’s, before the discovery of the applications.

This is fantastic, I would love to see Krohn-Rhodes make it in!

I'm not sure about reviewer expertise availability between Mathlib and CSLib, but I do hope the more mathematical parts are submitted to Mathlib.
